newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo 1997 trade gap seen widening.
newsitem.headline: Yugo 1997 trade gap seen widening.

text.p: Yugoslavia's trade deficit will continue to widen next year after topping $1.9 billion in the first 11 months of 1996, economists said on Friday.
Although the government has forecast a 47 percent increase in exports in 1997, economists doubted such robust growth could be achieved.
Milovan Zivkovic, head of the Federal Statistics Office, said 1997 exports will rise to $2.8 billion compared with a projected $1.8 billion this year.
But the Institute for Foreign Trade saw 1997 exports ranging between $2 billion and $2.5 billion with imports rising to between $5.8-$6 billion dollars.
"If the tendency continues, and there are no signs it may be reversed, the 1997 deficit will expand to at least $3.3 billion," Zivojin Jevtic of the Institute told Reuters.
Jevtic said exports picked up in November due to seasonal factors, but imports remained considerably higher.
Statistics showed November exports stood at $179 million and imports at $348 million. Exports for the first 11 months rose to $1.615 billion while imports soared to $3.576 billion.
"Yugoslavia has to maintain strong imports in 1997 to replace outdated technology and equipment," Jevtic added.

To reduce the deficit, Yugoslavia needed to restore bilateral ties with former trading partners, obtain membership of the World Trade Organisation and renew economic relations with former Yugoslavia's republics, the institute said.
Economists said Yugoslavia heavily relied on a $1 billion barter deal with China to revive its exports. But bilateral trade with China from January to November stood at only $53 million.
The deal with China, never precisely time-framed, envisaged exchanging Chinese oil for a variety of Yugoslav products.
China was eighth on the list of Yugoslavia's chief trading partners, behind France, Italy, Germany, United States, Russia, Ukraine and Belarus, Jevtic said.

"The moment the deal was announced, we warned it was an unnatural form of trading. It is desirable to some degree, but if barters were the best way to trade, the whole world would be in it," said Stojan Stamenkovic of the Institute of Economic Sciences.
Regardless of the deal with China, Yugoslavia may retain the trade gap as a constant feature of its economy, economists said.
"The deficit is not a consequence of an economic policy but a result of the structure of our economy," said Milojko Arsic of the private economic research institute CES-Mecon.
Government aims to see exports generating 50 percent of the GDP might be realised in seven or eight years, economists said.
But they agreed any sizeable exports growth depended on radical reforms and privatisation. Further delay in privatisation will put brakes on long-term economic performance, economists said.
